newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Ukraine says Chernobyl equipment needs checks.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine says Chernobyl equipment needs checks.

text.p: Ukraine's top nuclear official on Wednesday confirmed no increases in radiation or temperature had been registered at the Chernobyl nuclear plant but said a swift probe was needed to check monitoring equipment.

"No radiation or temperature changes were registered," Yuri Kostenko, Ukraine's Minister for Nuclear Safety, told Reuters during a conference in Vienna, contradicting remarks made by Chernobyl officials on Tuesday.

Officials at Chernobyl on Tuesday said there had been sharp increases in neutron activity and temperature inside the "sarcophagus" -- the protective casing erected after Chernobyl's fourth reactor exploded on April 26, 1986, sending a radioactive cloud over much of Europe.
But Kostenko said he was concerned that monitoring instruments placed in the plant after the explosion had registered a rise in temperature as well as neutron activity.

"If this situation was really registered and it was not a failure in the measurement, it indicates the situation in the sarcophagus has changed and we have to provide a very quick investigation," said Kostenko, who was attending the International Atomic Energy Agency's (IAEA) annual conference.
"We hope it is a mistake in the equipment, but the situation in the sarcophagus can provide this sort of neutron flux and I am worried because no one knows the real situation there."

Cash-strapped Ukraine is unable to raise the funds to conduct a thorough investigation of the Chernobyl sarcophagus and government officials had already approached the United States for financial help, Kostenko said.
"We need to review our investigations inside the sarcophagus but we have no money. We are now in contact with the U.S. government," the minister said.

Kostenko said Ukraine needed millions of dollars to upgrade the measuring equipment inside the now-defunct reactor, 140 km (90 miles) north of Kiev. "We'll need two to three millions just to get started," he said.
Regular inspections of the site ended four years ago when funds ran out, he said, and international technical expertise and funds were needed for further investigations to go ahead.

In Kiev, French nuclear safety expert Patrick Michaille said increased neutron radiation was probably caused by heavy rains but remained far below levels posing a public danger. He discounted faulty equipment as a cause.

"There is a remote chance that if it were repeated it could cause a chain reaction through an accumulation of nuclear fuel and moisture in some parts of the sarcophagus, but this is most improbable," Michaille said.
